group.passage:
For at least 3,000 years, smallpox was one of the most feared diseases on Earth. Caused by the variola virus, it killed about three in every ten people who caught it, and many of those who lived were left with deep scars or even blind. Today, no one catches it at all; it is the only human disease that has ever been completely wiped out.
Long before modern medicine, people in parts of Asia and Africa had learned that a mild case could guard against a deadly one. They took material from a patient’s sores and placed it in a scratch on a healthy person’s arm, which usually caused a milder illness but still relied on the real disease. In 1796, the English doctor Edward Jenner tried a safer path. Having noticed that milkmaids who had caught cowpox seemed to escape smallpox, he took matter from a cowpox sore on a milkmaid’s hand and gave it to an eight-year-old boy. When the boy was later exposed to smallpox, he stayed healthy. Since the Latin word for cow is vacca, the method came to be called vaccination.
By the middle of the twentieth century, vaccination had ended smallpox in North America, western Europe, and Japan. In 1959, the World Health Organization set out to remove it everywhere else, but the effort was held back by a lack of money, workers, and vaccine. A stronger campaign began in 1967, helped by a freeze-dried vaccine that did not need to be kept cold. Health workers also hunted for new cases, kept patients apart from others, and vaccinated everyone who had been close to them.
The disease itself made such a plan possible. The virus infected only humans, so it had no animals to hide in, and it did not stay quietly inside people for years. Patients also developed a clear rash, which made cases easy to spot. Smallpox was driven out of South America in 1971, out of Asia in 1975, and out of Africa in 1977. The last person to catch it in nature, a hospital cook in Somalia, recovered. A year later, a medical photographer in England died after being infected near a laboratory that studied the virus. In May 1980, the world was officially declared free of smallpox.

questions.stem: What is the passage mainly about?

options.A: How Edward Jenner turned an observation about milkmaids into a new method.
options.B: How a deadly disease was wiped out, and why that was possible.
options.C: Why smallpox killed more people than any other disease in history.
options.D: How the World Health Organization won quick support for its 1959 plan.

questions.stem: Which of the following questions can be answered from the passage?

options.A: Who was the first person to try variolation?
options.B: How many people did smallpox kill each year before 1967?
options.C: When did the last person who caught smallpox in nature die?
options.D: Why did the 1959 effort to end smallpox make slow progress?

questions.stem: Based on the passage, which kind of disease would be the hardest to wipe out with the methods used against smallpox?

options.A: One that also lives in animals and often shows no clear signs.
options.B: One that kills a larger share of the people who catch it.
options.C: One that causes a rash that makes its patients easy to spot.
options.D: One that is passed only from one person to another.

questions.stem: Why does the author mention the medical photographer in England?

options.A: To show that smallpox was still spreading among people in Europe.
options.B: To suggest that laboratories should stop keeping the smallpox virus.
options.C: To point out that one later case came from a laboratory, not nature.
options.D: To prove that the vaccine could not protect people who worked in labs.

translation_zh.text:
至少三千年來，天花一直是世上最令人畏懼的疾病之一。它由天花病毒（variola virus）引起，每十個染病的人大約有三個死亡，許多倖存者留下很深的疤痕，甚至失明。如今已經沒有人會得天花；它是人類至今唯一被完全根除的疾病。
早在現代醫學出現之前，亞洲與非洲部分地區的人就已經知道，得一次輕微的病可以防止得致命的病。他們從病人的膿瘡取出物質，放進健康者手臂上的抓痕裡；這種做法通常只會引起較輕微的病，但用的仍然是真正的天花。1796 年，英國醫師愛德華．金納（Edward Jenner）試了一條更安全的路。他注意到得過牛痘的擠奶女工似乎不會染上天花，於是從一名擠奶女工手上的牛痘膿瘡取出物質，接種給一名八歲男孩。這個男孩後來接觸天花，仍然安然無恙。由於拉丁文的「牛」是 vacca，這種方法後來就被稱為 vaccination（接種疫苗）。
到了二十世紀中葉，疫苗接種已經讓北美、西歐和日本不再有天花。1959 年，世界衛生組織著手在其他所有地方根除天花，但這項工作因為缺乏經費、人力和疫苗而受阻。1967 年展開了更有力的行動，冷凍乾燥、不需冷藏的疫苗幫了大忙。衛生人員也四處搜尋新病例，把病人和其他人隔開，並替所有和病人密切接觸過的人接種疫苗。
天花本身的特性也讓這樣的計畫可行。這種病毒只感染人類，所以沒有動物可以讓它藏身，也不會在人體內悄悄潛伏多年。此外，病人會出現明顯的疹子，病例很容易辨認。天花在 1971 年從南美洲、1975 年從亞洲、1977 年從非洲被驅逐。最後一位在自然狀況下染上天花的人是索馬利亞一名醫院廚師，他後來康復了。一年後，英國一名醫學攝影師在一間研究天花病毒的實驗室附近受到感染而死亡。1980 年 5 月，世界正式宣布天花絕跡。

open_tasks.prompt: Some diseases today are much harder to wipe out than smallpox was. Using one feature of smallpox from the passage, explain in 1–2 English sentences why that feature made the disease easier to end.
reference_answers: Smallpox infected only humans, so once every case was found and every contact was vaccinated, the virus had nowhere else to survive.
Smallpox patients developed a clear rash, so health workers could quickly find each case and vaccinate the people around it before the disease spread.

D.explanation_zh: 與文意相反：只在人與人之間傳播、沒有動物宿主，正是天花能被根除的原因之一，不會是最難根除的病。

A.evidence: By the middle of the twentieth century, vaccination had ended smallpox in North America, western Europe, and Japan.
A.explanation_zh: 英國屬於西歐，而文中說西歐在二十世紀中葉就已經沒有天花；攝影師是在研究病毒的實驗室附近被感染的單一病例，不是天花仍在歐洲人群中流行。改寫後這句只換了地名順序，仍然足以排除這個選項。

B.evidence: A year later, a medical photographer in England died after being infected near a laboratory that studied the virus.
B.explanation_zh: 作者只陳述攝影師在實驗室附近被感染而死亡的事件，全文沒有任何評論或建議，看不出作者主張實驗室不應保存病毒。

D.evidence: A year later, a medical photographer in England died after being infected near a laboratory that studied the virus.
D.explanation_zh: 文中沒有提到攝影師是否接種過疫苗，也沒有說疫苗對實驗室人員無效，無從「證明」這一點。
